title: CMOs Are Thinking Big with Agentic AI. They Should Be Thinking Even Bigger.
gist: A BCG/GMMA survey of ~60 CMOs (2026) finds AI in marketing shifting from efficiency pilots to scaled, cross-functional enterprise-value initiatives, with clear AI visions unlocking funding. Agentic AI is expected to rise from 7% to 27% of marketing teams in 2-3 years, squeezing agency and freelance labor and pushing agencies toward outcome-based partnership models.

themes.theme: C-suite pivots AI from cost to enterprise value

insights.claim: A BCG / Global Marketing and Media Alliance survey of about 60 CMOs (May-July 2026) finds the C-suite has moved beyond viewing AI mainly as a cost-reduction tool and now converges on AI as a driver of product innovation, enterprise value, and growth.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Vendors pitching AI on growth/revenue outcomes rather than headcount savings should find more receptive enterprise buyers.
insights.locator: The C-Suite Rallies Around Enterprise Value

insights.claim: The share of corporate AI initiatives focused solely on exploration fell nine percentage points to 11%, while cross-functional, at-scale initiatives grew six points to more than 21%; functional pilots remain the largest category at just over one-third.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Signals enterprise AI is shifting from experimentation budgets to scaled production spend, favoring platform and integration providers.
insights.quote: The center of gravity is moving decisively toward scale (growing six percentage points)
insights.locator: Now that leaders are more aligned

insights.claim: BCG argues that companies pushing toward end-to-end workflow reimagination and connecting data and decisions across silos are more likely to create enterprise value than those making functional 'assembly lines' more efficient with discrete AI use cases.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Favors cross-silo data/decisioning infrastructure over point-solution AI tools.
insights.quote: not simply making functional “assembly lines” more efficient
insights.locator: The mix of AI initiatives reflects a maturation

insights.claim: CMOs remain somewhat isolated in AI thinking, prioritizing marketing effectiveness and customer-journey connection while C-suite peers articulate enterprise-wide priorities; personalization is the common ground between marketing and technology leaders.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Personalization tooling is the likeliest budget overlap between marketing and IT, a natural wedge for martech vendors.
insights.locator: CMOs, however, remain somewhat isolated

insights.claim: 73% of CMOs expect AI's most tangible marketing impact in marketing effectiveness and another 73% in operational efficiency, while 41% also cite budget reinvestment and new sources of growth.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Efficiency remains the near-term AI payoff in marketing, but a sizable minority already budget for growth uses.
insights.locator: For marketing specifically, CMOs expect AI

themes.theme: Vision clarity as a funding strategy

insights.claim: 64% of CMOs say accelerating AI-enabled marketing transformation is a bigger part of their job, almost half are focused on redesigning the marketing operating model, and 38% are driving enterprise-wide transformation.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: The CMO mandate is expanding into enterprise transformation, enlarging the buyer persona for AI and consulting services.
insights.locator: Shifting CMO Leadership Roles

insights.claim: CMOs with a mature, well-articulated AI vision are far more likely to report enough or more than enough funding (62%), while 63% of those with a less clear vision say they need a little or a lot more funding — clarity of ambition itself acts as a funding strategy.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Organizations with articulated AI roadmaps are likelier to sustain AI budgets; watch for vision-led spending as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: clarity of ambition itself can be a funding strategy
insights.locator: As the job expands, having a clear vision

insights.claim: Funding for AI in marketing comes roughly half from marketing's own budgets and half from nonmarketing sources such as enterprise transformation funds, CEO/CFO budgets, and external partners, meaning it is increasingly treated as an enterprise investment rather than a functional line item.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Marketing AI spend is less exposed to marketing budget cuts because half is underwritten by enterprise pools.
insights.locator: Funding comes from a mix of sources

themes.theme: Workflow disruption: media more than creative

insights.claim: In creative workflows, marketers expect adaptation, personalization, and creative testing to be the most disrupted by AI in the next two to three years, with human-AI collaboration opportunities in upstream ideation, hero asset creation, derivative production, and asset management.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Creative-versioning and testing tools are the most exposed segment of creative services to AI substitution.
insights.locator: Substantial Disruptions in End-to-End Workflows

insights.claim: Marketers expect more fundamental AI disruption in media workflows than creative ones, particularly in measurement, optimization, and planning, while judgment-heavy work like business planning and media strategy will be less affected.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Media measurement and optimization services face the greatest automation pressure; strategy work holds value.
insights.locator: Marketers expect even more fundamental disruption in media

insights.claim: Performance media and CRM use cases such as email are identified as among the most ripe for AI disruption across content types and channels.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Performance marketing agencies and email/CRM service providers are frontline exposure to agentic substitution.
insights.quote: Performance media and key marketing use cases in customer relationship management, such as email, are among the most ripe for AI disruption.
insights.locator: In general, performance media and key marketing

themes.theme: Agencies squeezed by technology and in-housing

insights.claim: Agency accountability for marketing work is expected to decline 9% to 13% across creative and media workflows, while internal marketing teams' accountability grew 6% and technology's share rose 7% (creative) and 6% (media), though these shifts are more moderate than forecasts a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Structural headwind for agency holding companies' revenue base, but the pace of erosion is slower than last year's expectations.
insights.locator: Accountability Is Shifting Among People, Technology, and Partners

insights.claim: Three-quarters of CMOs say their creative agencies are not prepared to scale AI (an 11-point improvement year over year), while 73% say media agencies are not AI-ready, up 6 points — media agencies are losing ground on AI readiness.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Media agencies appear more at risk of share loss than creative agencies given deteriorating perceived AI readiness.
insights.locator: Agencies are still a vital part of the mix

insights.claim: CMOs' top asks of agencies are investment in AI technology and upskilling, followed by different talent, leadership, and structure, and increasingly revised commercial models.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Expect agency pricing to migrate away from FTE-based fees; watch holding-company AI capex and outcome-based contracts.
insights.locator: Investment in AI technology and upskilling remain the top asks

insights.claim: CMOs expect AI in marketing to be sourced 24% from frontier AI and cloud providers, 21% from media owners, 21% from martech/enterprise tech providers, 18% from internally built solutions, 10% from disruptive or point solutions, and 7% from independent agencies and disruptors.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Frontier model/cloud vendors and media owners capture the largest share of marketing AI supply; agencies capture little.
insights.locator: The survey also showed that AI in marketing

insights.claim: BCG recommends CMOs rebuild agency relationships around shared outcomes and value rather than transactional FTE/time-based models, with tight internal-external handoffs as agentic AI operates on both sides of the boundary.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Agencies that cannot move to outcome-based pricing risk disintermediation.
insights.quote: constructed around shared outcomes and value rather than transactional, FTE/time-based models of the past
insights.locator: AI disruption is a chance for CMOs

themes.theme: Agentic AI reshapes the marketing talent mix

insights.claim: Agentic AI accounts for 7% of the marketing team mix and is expected to nearly quadruple to 27% within two to three years, faster than anticipated a year ago.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Accelerating agentic adoption expands the market for agent platforms and orchestration tooling in marketing.
insights.locator: Agentic AI Demands a New Talent and Partnership Model

insights.claim: CMOs expect agentic AI gains to come unevenly from human categories: agency talent falling from 25% to 16% of the mix, freelance from 8% to 5%, and full-timers from 57% to 48%, with the in-house core remaining the largest component.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Agency and freelance labor bear disproportionate displacement; freelance marketplaces and agencies face volume pressure.
insights.locator: Agentic AI's future gains are forecasted

insights.claim: On a five-point scale, CMOs anticipate the human talent mix shifting toward more senior talent (2.6) and slightly toward in-house over outsourced (2.3), while staying balanced between marketers and technologists, creatives and scientists, and generalists and specialists (3.0 each).
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Junior execution roles are the most exposed; demand shifts toward senior strategic marketers.
insights.locator: As agentic AI constitutes more of the “team,”

insights.claim: BCG contends AI will not simply displace people in specific marketing roles but requires fundamental redesign of workflows and accountability, with the talent agenda extending beyond upskilling to leadership, role definition, structure, partnerships, and incentives.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: Change-management and operating-model redesign services stand to benefit alongside AI tooling.
insights.locator: Our research bolsters the argument

insights.claim: BCG's four recommended CMO actions are: think bigger (lead AI-driven growth across the enterprise), articulate the AI vision explicitly (as both funding and execution strategy), embrace a hybrid human-agentic workforce, and rewire the operating model with agencies into a seamless internal-external continuum.
insights.speaker: Janet Balis
insights.so_what: A checklist for assessing whether a company's marketing organization is positioned to capture AI-driven growth.
insights.locator: The Path Forward
